commentary.bottom_line: Seven small offline or simulated studies suggest that letting clinicians edit, reject, or reweight AI outputs may improve output accuracy and catch some model errors, but no study tested a defined override rule or a logged disagreement process in live care. The certainty that the full practice improves patient outcomes is very low.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are level 4 or 5 and offline or simulated. Patient-level samples ranged from 12 plans to 29 patients, one vignette study enrolled 22 physicians, one benchmark used 11,748 images, and one study did not report sample size. Each favored human correction, but imprecision, indirectness, and no test of required-override rules or logging support a very low rating.

Surgeons rejected AI suggestions in 9 of 13 false-positive cases, which means 4 errors passed through review. The contestable interface caught only a portion of model errors. These results suggest override access intercepts some errors but not all, and no study measured whether corrected outputs changed harm reaching patients.

Manual editing raised Dice agreement to 0.84 from 0.60 and 0.55, and raised prostate contours to 0.86 from 0.82. Adjustable weights were rated 4.18 versus 3.41 for static weights. One hazard study found readers had difficulty correcting slice-level annotations, which suggests interface design affects whether override is usable. No study reported editing time or workload.

A European pathology society paper reads the EU AI Act as requiring manual override mechanisms, and the CHAI guide lists user override as a must. These endorsements set expectations for vendors and purchasers, but none of the supplied studies tests whether meeting them changes outcomes.

Five tests were run in the United Kingdom, Italy, Russia, Japan, and a mixed Israel, USA, and Canada physician sample, and two did not report setting. None described patient insurance, language, or literacy, so the evidence cannot show whether override tools perform equally across populations.

Every test gave the correction power to clinicians or experts. No study examined whether patients could contest an AI output or learn that a clinician had overridden one, so the evidence says nothing about patient trust or access to a human reviewer.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested a defined threshold for when override is required, a logged disagreement workflow, or the downstream use of override logs, and none has measured patient outcomes, clinician time burden, or override rates in live clinical deployment.
commentary.underserved_note: No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so whether override and contest mechanisms work for these patients and the clinicians serving them remains unknown.
